first.rationale: The two declining metrics (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) point at the same funnel stage, and simplifying onboarding is the one lever that plausibly moves both while being cheap and reversible. I am verifying memory_31 and memory_86 because they are the two memories I would actually lean on and they may not be independent: 'shortening onboarding' (day 52) and 'cutting required fields at signup' (day 31) could easily be two consolidations of one underlying experiment, which would mean my apparent corroboration is really a single result counted twice. If the archive shows they are one source, I keep the direction but treat the effect size as unproven and hold the test guarded rather than assuming a durable lift. I deliberately did not spend budget on memory_73 even though promotional pricing is the obvious reflex against the competitor's entry pricing: its defect is already disclosed on the face of the memory (pooled cohorts after a mid-test redefinition), so the readout cannot be cited as a clean effect regardless of what the archive says, and discount-led acquisition is the direction most likely to buy short-term signups at the cost of the primary objective — sustainable long-term qualified revenue. That is the main downstream value risk here: matching a competitor on price would reprice the SMB base, attract the least retentive cohort, and be hard to unwind, whereas a funnel fix compounds. Referral incentives (memory_57) and enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) are credible but address segments that are not the ones currently bleeding. Activation messaging (memory_91) is the strongest fallback and I would run it next if onboarding verification collapses. Uncertainty preserved: all six memories are archived prior readouts under different market conditions, and none were measured against an active price-aggressive competitor, so prior effect sizes should be treated as directional rather than predictive.
